new_items.title: Evolutionary repurposing of a pore-forming toxin drives epithelial remodeling during terrestrial adaptation.
new_items.summary_rss: The ability of vertebrates to conquer land is attributed to innovations in respiration and locomotion. However, land adaptation profoundly reshaped mucosal surfaces such as the skin, the main interface between hosts and the environment. To adapt to land, African lungfish annually remodel their skin, forming a cocoon. Here, we report the discovery of a small pore-forming toxin in African lungfish, Protop-CrTX-A, with no other vertebrate counterpart that is sufficient to drive epithelial morphogenesis transcriptional programs. In free-swimming lungfish, goblet cells secrete Protop-CrTX-A into the mucus. During estivation, this niche is replaced by a mucin-low/basal epithelial niche, adjacent to a granulocyte immune niche that becomes the predominant source of Protop-CrTX-A in the estivated skin. Protop-CrTX-A acts as a reversible switch for skin remodeling, sufficient to convert African lungfish skin between aquatic and terrestrial states. We propose that innate immunity, through its capacity to remodel tissues, was a key driver of vertebrate water-land transitions.

new_items.title: Paleogenomics illuminates mobility and changing lifeways in Chalcolithic Anatolia.
new_items.summary_rss: Once labeled the "Dark Ages" of Anatolian prehistory, the Chalcolithic period (c. 6000-3000 BCE) was characterized by drastically reduced settlement densities compared with the preceding Neolithic and the succeeding Bronze Ages, a change interpreted as population decline. Using 44 new genomes combined with published data, we find no evidence for a population reduction. The genetic evidence instead suggests that populations in Chalcolithic Anatolia were increasingly mobile and/or growing in size while receiving gene flow from eastern regions (e.g., East Anatolia and the South Caucasus) through a 3,000-year-long admixture process. We propose that genetic and archaeological evidence may be reconciled by hypothesizing the presence of communities with dispersed and mobile lifeways that are mostly invisible to archaeology. These communities also practiced consanguinity at frequencies unobserved in previous periods. Finally, we identify a mid-5th-millennium BCE individual in Central Anatolia carrying ∼10%-30% Pontic-Caspian Steppe-related ancestry, shedding light on mobility between the Eurasian Steppe and Anatolia.
